KEY MESSAGE 1...A cool and wet start to meteorological fall. Some 
rain could be heavy, leading to poor drainage flooding.

The backdoor cold front that pushed southwest of New England this 
morning starts to shift back to the northeast today, with increasing 
cloud cover this afternoon. As advertised the past several days, 
there are multiple rounds of beneficial rainfall this week, with the 
first round coming late tonight through Tuesday. With the frontal 
boundary shifting northeast, PWATs increase to between 1.8-2.0 
inches, interacting with a weak wave of low pressure riding along 
the boundary.

Timing-wise, rain aims to arrive around midnight west of the CT 
River Valley and around the time of the Tuesday morning commute for 
the I-95 corridor. Looking at BUFKIT, do see warm rain processes 
with the warm cloud layer around 10k feet. Locally heavy downpours, 
especially during the daytime Tuesday, are possible, which may lead 
to localized street and poor drainage flooding. This coincides with 
the Day 1-2 ERO Marginal Risk (level 1 out of 4) for excessive 
rainfall.

Do think there will be a thin axis of heaviest rainfall across the 
southwest section of our CWA. Rainfall amounts are in the 
neighborhood of half an inch to an inch, with lesser amounts east of 
I-95, where totals are in the range of a quarter to half an inch. 
Since these are showers versus stratiform rain, there could be areas 
of higher and lower amounts within a relatively short distance. 
However, a subtle shift northeast could put some of the heaviest 
rainfall across parts of central Massachusetts and eastern 
Connecticut. Additionally, there's a lower chance for thunder, 
mainly Tuesday afternoon, with a few hundred J/kg of CAPE across 
mainly western Massachusetts and Connecticut, although it's not a 
significant risk.

Rain tapers off late Tuesday, with drier conditions overspreading 
the region Tuesday night into early Thursday morning. Given the 
clouds, expect a much cooler start to Tuesday, with highs mainly in 
the upper 60s to lower 70s. A true nod to the first day of 
meteorological fall.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Unsettled weather late Wed into Thursday, with 
several rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Low confidence on exact 
timing. 

1025 mb high pressure over the Maritimes should provide dry weather 
much of Wed, especially across eastern MA, while a frontal boundary 
lurks to the west and southwest of SNE. This front will eventually 
move northeast as a warm front later Wed and especially Wed night, 
resulting in an increased risk for showers and thunderstorms across 
SNE late Wed/Wed night. Cooler temps Wed, with 1025 Maritime high 
and ESE onshore flow, limiting max temps in the upper 60s and lower 
70s.

Trailing/secondary short wave and associated cold front impact the 
region around Thu. Potential for thunderstorms to become strong to 
severe during this time, as warm sector airmass overspreads SNE. 
However, better instability/higher theta-e airmass appears to remain 
southwest of SNE. Thus, potential for severe weather and flash 
flooding here looks limited at this time range. Heat and humidity 
return Thu with warm sector airmass, highs in the lower 80s and dew 
pts in the upper 60s and lower 70s. 

  
KEY MESSAGE 3...Improving weather Friday and into the holiday 
weekend. Other than a spot diurnal shower each day, dry weather 
prevails with a mix of clouds and sun. Cooler than normal with highs 
in the 70s and lows in the 50s, along with onshore breezes.

Definitely a sign of fall approaching, with robust northern stream 
Friday yielding a baroclinic 998 mb maritime low late Fri/Sat. This 
will yield a cool, brisk NE flow into the SNE over the weekend. 
Highs likely remaining in the 70s and overnight lows in the 50s. It 
will feel even cooler over southeast MA, including Cape Cod and the 
Islands, with northeast winds 15-25 mph. Cool cyclonic flow aloft 
will yield diurnal clouds each day and possibly a spot shower. 
Otherwise, dry weather prevails. Possibly warmer and less wind for 
Memorial Day Monday, as high amplitude trough moves offshore and 
1025 mb high settles over SNE.
